key_insight: Video-LLMs suffer from a systematic failure — "directional motion blindness" — where they cannot reliably report simple signed image-plane motion (left/right/up/down); above-chance answers are largely driven by prediction biases rather than true motion understanding.
problem_solved: Diagnoses why modern Video-LLMs fail to perceive basic motion direction and presents targeted evaluation and remediation strategies to restore genuine directional motion sensitivity.
method: Design controlled, single-object motion probes (left/right/up/down) to isolate directional perception from semantic/contextual cues.
Quantitatively evaluate popular Video-LLMs, trace error patterns and prediction biases to localize the failure mode (directional motion blindness).

Propose and validate interventions to overcome the blindness (bias-controlled evaluation, targeted training/finetuning and motion-augmented inputs such as optical-flow or temporal attention enhancements).
impact: Clarifies a fundamental perceptual limitation in Video-LLMs and provides practical evaluation and mitigation techniques, improving reliability for downstream tasks that depend on accurate motion perception (e.g., robotics, autonomous systems, video analytics).
visual_elements: Four-panel schematic showing a single object moving left, right, up, down (ground truth labels).
Bar chart comparing model accuracy to chance and showing how much above-chance performance is explained by bias.
Confusion matrix or Sankey diagram visualizing systematic mispredictions and bias directions.
Before/after diagram showing model input or training change (e.g., raw frames → frames+optical-flow or finetuned model) and corresponding accuracy lift.
paper_title: Which Way Did It Move? Diagnosing and Overcoming Directional Motion Blindness in Video-LLMs
paper_authors: Jongseo Lee, Hyuntak Lee, Sunghun Kim, Sooa Kim, Jihoon Chung
